findings.description: The retry wrapper now reuses one statistics dict for every call and clears it on entry, and the copy's _local.statistics is pointed at that same dict. A nested or recursive call through the same wrapped function therefore clears and overwrites the outer call's statistics while the outer call is still running.
findings.rationale: Trigger: a @retry-decorated function that calls itself, or calls the same wrapped function again, while an outer call is still retrying. The inner call runs stats.clear() on the dict the outer loop is still writing attempt_number and related fields into, and both copies share that dict. Impact: the outer call's statistics are reset or replaced by the inner call's values, so wrapped_f.statistics reports wrong attempt counts. The previous code gave each call its own dict to prevent exactly this.

findings.description: The async wrapper has the same shared-dict pattern: it clears the dict and binds the copy's and the outer local's statistics to it, so concurrent or nested invocations of the same decorated coroutine share and clobber one statistics dict.
findings.rationale: Trigger: two overlapping awaits of the same @retry-decorated coroutine, or a recursive await of it. Each invocation calls stats.clear() on the shared dict and then writes attempt_number and timing fields into it. Impact: each caller reads statistics that belong to another in-flight call, and the values are wrong or reset mid-call. The old code rebinding a fresh copy.statistics per call avoided this.
